comp.label: The Night the River Came Up
comp.compStory:
The warning came at four o'clock, not as a siren but as a rumour. It travelled along Mill Street faster than the rain itself: the river had climbed over the stone steps by the bridge, and it was still climbing. By the time it reached the bakery, it had grown teeth.

"They're saying the whole lower town will go under," announced Mrs Okafor from the doorway, shaking her umbrella so fiercely that she seemed to be punishing it.

Behind the counter, Gran did not look up from the dough she was folding. "They said that in 1998," she replied. "And the river only came as far as the post office. It is a river, Mrs Okafor. It has no ambition."

Leo, who had been sent to the bakery after school because his parents were both working late, said nothing. He was eleven, and he had learned that when adults argued in that particular polite tone, it was wisest to become furniture. Still, he edged towards the window. Mill Street had turned the colour of strong tea, and the drains were no longer swallowing the rain but coughing it back up.

By six, the rumour had become a fact. Water slid under the front door in a thin, glittering sheet. Gran finally put down the dough.

"Right," she said, and the single word did the work of a whole speech. "Flour sacks onto the top shelves. Then the till. Then the photographs."

Leo had always thought of the photographs as wallpaper. They hung in a crooked line above the ovens: men in flat caps, women with floury forearms, a boy no older than Leo holding a loaf almost as long as himself. He had walked past them a thousand times without looking. Now, lifting them down one by one, he found he could not stop looking.

"Who's this?" he asked, holding up the boy with the enormous loaf.

"Your great-grandfather, Arthur. That was taken the week he started here. He was twelve, and he hated every minute of it, to begin with."

"Why did he stay, then?"

Gran was quiet for so long that Leo thought she had not heard. The water was ankle-deep now and bitterly cold.

"Because one winter," she said at last, "the mill flooded and there was no bread anywhere in the town except here. Arthur's father kept the ovens going for three days, and people queued in the snow. Arthur said it was the first time he understood that a bakery isn't really about bread."

"What is it about, then?"

"You'll work it out," said Gran, which was what she always said when she wanted him to think rather than ask.

At half past seven, a man in a fluorescent jacket knocked on the window and told them, through the glass, that they must leave. Gran nodded politely, as though he were a customer asking the price of scones, and turned back to the ovens.

"Gran, he said we have to go."

"He said the street has to go," Gran corrected him. "The ovens are on the raised floor at the back. They'll stay dry for hours yet. And in the morning, there will be a great many people with wet kitchens and no breakfast."

Leo opened his mouth to argue and then, slowly, closed it again. He thought of Arthur at twelve, hating every minute. He thought of a queue of people in the snow. Somewhere inside his chest, something shifted, like a key turning in a stiff lock.

"What do you need me to do?"

Gran looked at him properly then: not the quick, checking look she gave him when he came in from school, but a long, measuring one, the kind she gave dough when she was deciding whether it was ready.

"Knead," she said, and pushed a bowl towards him.

They worked through the night. The river grumbled against the front of the shop like a dog that had been shut out, but it came no further than the second step of the raised floor. At dawn, as the water began its sulky retreat, the first neighbours appeared: Mrs Okafor, still clutching her umbrella; the man in the fluorescent jacket, looking sheepish; children in wellingtons with coats pulled over their pyjamas.

Leo handed out loaves until his arms ached. Nobody paid. Nobody was asked to.

Later, when the photographs were back on their hooks, a little more crooked than before, Leo stood in front of the picture of Arthur for a long time.

"I've worked it out," he told Gran.

She did not ask him what the answer was. She simply smiled and handed him a broom.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: At what time did the warning about the river first reach Mill Street?
questions.optionA: Half past seven
questions.optionB: Seven o'clock
questions.optionD: Six o'clock
questions.optionE: Dawn
questions.explanation: The first line says the warning came at four o'clock.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "By the time it reached the bakery, it had grown teeth." What does this suggest about the rumour?
questions.optionA: It had travelled more slowly than the rain
questions.optionB: It had become more alarming as it spread
questions.optionC: It had been proved to be false
questions.optionD: It had been started by a dog
questions.optionE: It had turned into a joke
questions.explanation: Saying the rumour had 'grown teeth' means it had become fiercer and more frightening as it was passed on.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Mrs Okafor shook her umbrella "so fiercely that she seemed to be punishing it". What does this show about her?
questions.optionA: She was angry that her umbrella was broken
questions.optionB: She wanted to dry the umbrella before the shop closed
questions.optionD: She was agitated and worked up about the news
questions.optionE: She was trying to make Gran laugh
questions.explanation: The violent shaking reflects how stirred up and anxious she is about the flood rumour.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: When Gran says the river "has no ambition", what is her view at first?
questions.optionA: She is afraid of what Mrs Okafor will do
questions.optionB: She thinks it is the most dangerous river in the country
questions.optionC: She thinks the river is beautiful
questions.optionD: She believes it is unlikely to rise much further
questions.optionE: She is planning to leave town
questions.explanation: She compares it with 1998, when the water stopped at the post office, and dismisses the idea that it will go further.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Leo had learned that it was "wisest to become furniture". What does he decide to do?
questions.optionA: Hide underneath the counter
questions.optionB: Keep quiet so that the adults do not notice him
questions.optionC: Help to move the furniture away from the door
questions.optionD: Sit on a chair by the counter
questions.optionE: Leave the bakery and go home
questions.explanation: Furniture is silent and unnoticed; Leo stays out of the polite argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The drains were "coughing it back up". Which technique is the writer using here?
questions.optionA: Simile
questions.optionB: Alliteration
questions.optionD: Onomatopoeia
questions.optionE: Personification
questions.explanation: The drains are given a human action (coughing), which is personification.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "The single word did the work of a whole speech." What does this tell us about Gran's word "Right"?
questions.optionA: Leo could not hear what she said
questions.optionB: She went on to give a long speech
questions.optionC: She was cross with Mrs Okafor
questions.optionD: It showed clearly that she had decided to take charge
questions.optionE: She was confused about what to do
questions.explanation: One word was enough to signal her decision and set everyone to work, as a speech might.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How did Leo's attitude to the photographs change during the evening?
questions.optionA: He had always loved them and wanted to hang more
questions.optionB: His attitude did not change at all
questions.optionC: He became frightened of them and hid them
questions.optionD: He had barely noticed them before, but now he could not stop looking
questions.optionE: He decided they were ugly and old-fashioned
questions.explanation: He had treated them 'as wallpaper', but lifting them down he 'could not stop looking'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How old was Arthur when the photograph of him was taken?
questions.optionA: Fourteen
questions.optionB: Thirteen
questions.optionD: Ten
questions.optionE: Eleven
questions.explanation: Gran says, 'He was twelve.' (Leo is the one who is eleven.)

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to Gran, why did Arthur stay at the bakery?
questions.optionA: The mill closed and there was no other work
questions.optionB: His father paid him more than the mill did
questions.optionC: He realised it helped the whole town during a crisis
questions.optionD: He enjoyed queuing in the snow
questions.optionE: He wanted to be in more photographs
questions.explanation: When the mill flooded, the bakery was the town's only bread; Arthur understood it was about more than bread.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does Gran answer "You'll work it out" instead of explaining?
questions.optionA: She wants Leo to think about it for himself
questions.optionB: She wants him to look it up later
questions.optionC: She is annoyed by his questions
questions.optionD: She does not know the answer
questions.optionE: She is too busy to talk
questions.explanation: The text says this is what she said 'when she wanted him to think rather than ask'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did Gran refuse to leave when the man in the fluorescent jacket told them to go?
questions.optionA: She wanted to protect the photographs
questions.optionB: She was frightened of going out in the rain
questions.optionC: She thought the man was being rude
questions.optionD: She could not hear him through the glass
questions.optionE: She knew the ovens would stay dry and people would need bread in the morning
questions.explanation: She explains the ovens are on a raised floor and that many people will have 'no breakfast'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Something shifted, like a key turning in a stiff lock." What does this suggest is happening to Leo?
questions.optionA: He is starting to feel unwell
questions.optionB: He is worried about being locked in
questions.optionC: He has found the key to the shop
questions.optionD: He is becoming angry with Gran
questions.optionE: He is beginning to understand and change his mind
questions.explanation: A key turning opens something; Leo's understanding opens up and he offers to help.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Gran gave Leo "a long, measuring" look. Which is closest in meaning to "measuring" here?
questions.optionA: Counting quickly
questions.optionB: Weighing out
questions.optionD: Hurried
questions.optionE: Unfriendly
questions.explanation: She is assessing him, as she judges whether dough is ready.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The river "grumbled against the front of the shop like a dog that had been shut out". What impression does this give?
questions.optionA: The river was growing more dangerous every minute
questions.optionB: The river had gone completely silent
questions.optionC: The river was restless but could no longer get in
questions.optionD: The river was friendly and playful
questions.optionE: The river had already dried up
questions.explanation: A shut-out dog grumbles at the door but stays outside; the water came no further than the second step.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why did the man in the fluorescent jacket look "sheepish" at dawn?
questions.optionA: He was embarrassed, having told them to leave, yet now he had come for bread
questions.optionB: He was angry that the shop was still open
questions.optionC: He had lost his fluorescent jacket
questions.optionD: He was cold after working all night
questions.optionE: He was too tired to speak
questions.explanation: Sheepish means embarrassed; he benefits from the decision he had told them not to make.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What has Leo "worked out" by the end of the story?
questions.optionA: How to stop a river from flooding
questions.optionB: How to bake bread without an oven
questions.optionC: That a bakery is really about looking after the community
questions.optionD: That Gran had been wrong about the river
questions.optionE: That the photographs should hang straight
questions.explanation: It answers his earlier question: like Arthur, he sees the bakery serves people in need.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer end the story with Gran handing Leo a broom?
questions.optionA: To explain how the flood was cleaned up
questions.optionB: To show quietly that Gran now treats him as a real helper and the work goes on
questions.optionC: To show that the shop is closing down
questions.optionD: To show that Gran is cross with Leo
questions.optionE: To make the reader laugh at Leo
questions.explanation: The understated ending suggests acceptance: she doesn't need to ask his answer, she trusts him with the work.

questions.quest: The shape is made of rectangles and all corners are right angles. What is its area?

questions.optionB: 56 cm²

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A train leaves at 09:47 and arrives at 11:22. How long is the journey?
questions.optionA: 1 h 35 min
questions.optionB: 1 h 45 min
questions.optionD: 1 h 75 min
questions.optionE: 2 h 35 min
questions.explanation: 09:47 to 10:47 is 1 hour; 10:47 to 11:22 is 35 minutes.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 0.6 × 0.07?
questions.explanation: 6 × 7 = 42 and there are three decimal places in total: 0.042.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Two angles of a triangle are 48° and 67°. What is the third angle?
questions.explanation: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°: 180 − 48 − 67 = 65°.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Pens cost 35p each and pencils cost 18p each. Sam buys 6 pens and 5 pencils and pays with a £5 note. How much change does he get?
questions.explanation: 6 × 35p = £2.10 and 5 × 18p = 90p. Total £3.00; change from £5 is £2.00.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Round 47,368 to the nearest thousand.
questions.explanation: The hundreds digit is 3 (less than 5), so it rounds down to 47,000.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A cube has a volume of 125 cm³. What is its total surface area?
questions.optionA: 25 cm²
questions.optionB: 150 cm²
questions.optionD: 125 cm²
questions.optionE: 75 cm²
questions.explanation: The side is 5 cm (5 × 5 × 5 = 125). Each face is 25 cm² and there are 6 faces: 150 cm².

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the sum of all the prime numbers between 20 and 40?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: The point (3, −2) is reflected in the x-axis. What are the coordinates of its image?
questions.explanation: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y: (3, 2).

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 4 green counters. One is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT blue?
questions.explanation: 12 counters, 7 of which are not blue: 7/12.

questions.quest: In a code, FROST is written as HTQUV. How would BLANK be written in the same code?

questions.optionB: DNCPL
questions.optionD: ZJYLI
questions.optionE: DNCPM

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, MOTHER is written as NPUIFS. What does the code UBCMF stand for?
questions.optionA: FABLE
questions.optionB: CABLE
questions.optionD: SABLE
questions.optionE: TABLE
questions.explanation: Each code letter is one place after the real letter, so move each back one: U→T, B→A, C→B, M→L, F→E.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next pair in the series: AZ, CX, EV, GT, ?
questions.optionA: JR
questions.optionB: HS
questions.optionD: IS
questions.optionE: IR
questions.explanation: The first letter moves forward two each time (A, C, E, G, I); the second moves back two (Z, X, V, T, R).

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 3, 4, 7, 11, 18, 29, ?
questions.explanation: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 18 + 29 = 47.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 20, 17, 19, 16, 18, ?
questions.explanation: The pattern is −3, +2, −3, +2, so next is 18 − 3 = 15.

A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"Make sure the attic door is shut."

questions.optionB: attic door
questions.optionD: door is
questions.optionE: Make sure

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
A four-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"Thomas eats his lunch quickly."
questions.optionA: his lunch
questions.optionB: eats his
questions.optionD: lunch quickly
questions.optionE: None of these

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is closest in meaning to RELUCTANT?
questions.optionA: exhausted
questions.optionB: silent
questions.optionD: eager
questions.optionE: unwilling
questions.explanation: Reluctant means not wanting to do something: unwilling.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word is most nearly the OPPOSITE of SCARCE?
questions.optionA: rare
questions.optionB: plentiful
questions.optionD: tiny
questions.optionE: hidden
questions.explanation: Scarce means in short supply; the opposite is plentiful.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word does NOT belong with the others?
questions.optionA: ash
questions.optionB: tulip
questions.optionD: willow
questions.optionE: oak
questions.explanation: Oak, birch, willow and ash are trees; a tulip is a flower.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Which word can go in front of all of these to make three new words?  ___ball   ___flake   ___man
questions.optionA: snow
questions.optionB: sun
questions.optionD: foot
questions.optionE: rain
questions.explanation: snowball, snowflake, snowman. (Foot works for football only.)

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Bird is to nest as bee is to ?
questions.optionA: wing
questions.optionB: hive
questions.optionD: honey
questions.optionE: sting
questions.explanation: A nest is where a bird lives; a hive is where a bee lives.

brave   branch   bread   brand   bracket

questions.optionA: I

questions.optionE: S
questions.explanation: Taking L from SPLIT leaves SPIT; adding it to CAN makes CLAN.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: The words MATE, TAME and TEAM are written in a number code. The codes, in no particular order, are 5926, 2956 and 2695. What is the code for MEAT?
questions.explanation: TAME and TEAM both start with T, so 2 = T; the code starting 5 is MATE (5926), giving M=5, A=9, T=2, E=6. MEAT = 5692.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If A = 3, B = 5, C = 2, D = 10 and E = 6, what is (D × C) − (A × E)? Give your answer as a letter.

questions.optionB: B
questions.optionD: D

questions.subject: VERBAL
